full_judgment:
Muhammad Ansar Ali, J: This application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure by the defendants petitioners is directed against two orders namely order No 110 dated 18. 3. 1995 and order No 112 dated 2.4. 1995 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, lit Court, Chittagong in other Suit No 169 of 1985 asking first the defendant petitioners to cross examine P.W.1 one Omar Faruque Chowdhury and thereafter rejecting the application of the Petitioners under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for vacating the said order respectively. Facts relevant for the disposal of the application may briefly be stated as follows: 

2 Opposite parties No 1-6 and with some others instituted a suit being other suit No 169 of 1985 in the court of the 1st Subordinate Judge, Chittagong against the present defendant petitioners and some other defendants for the following reliefs: 

a) that a decree be passed declaring that the plaintiffs are entitled to the compensation money assured for the schedule land in L. A Misc. Case No 128 of 1983 -84 (Misc. Case No 2/1984-85) 

b) that the cost of the suit be decreed against the contesting defendants

c) that any other relief to which the plaintiffs are deemed entitled to.

3. The case of the plaintiffs opposite parties herein is interalia that the original owner of the land mentioned in tic schedule below was one Ramjan Ali and that C .S Khatian No 23 was finally published in his name. The said Ramjan Ali died leaving behind two sons namely Gura Miah and Syed Ali and two daughters namely, Sabur Khatun and Sadar Nisa alias Khatuni as his legal heirs. That during the time of R. S operation the said two daughters of Ramjan Ali were at their husbands house for which their names could not be recorded in the R S Khatians. But in spite of that they were in joint possession with their brothers Syed Ali and Gura Miah and. that the said Sadar Nisa alias Khatuni, Syed Ali, Thanda Miah, Abul Khatun and Tambia Khatun sold out 2.00 acres of land to plaintiff No 1 for their legal necessity including the schedule land vide registered kabala dated 9. 5. 1966 and delivered possession thereof to him and since the date of purchase the plaintiff No 1 is in peaceful possession of the same by paying rents, revenues etc. to the Government. Then he filed a Mutation Case No 572/11 of 1967-68 before the Circle Officer Hathazari, Chittagong who ordered for mutation of his name in S A Record but subsequently it was lost. Similarly the plaintiff No 2 also purchased .80 acre of land vide Registered kabala deeds dated 23.1.1984 and the plaintiff No 3 purchased .20 acre of land vide Registered kabala deed dated 23.1.1984 from one Bazal Ahmed, Oli Ahmed, Kabir Ahmed, Thanda Meah, Abul Khatun, Saleh Ahmed and Nur Begum on payment of proper consideration money and since then they are in peaceful possession of their purchased lands including .15 acre of the schedule land on payment of rent, to the Government. That the names of the plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3 were also recorded in the S.A Khatian through Mutation and the names of all the plaintiffs subsequently were recorded in present revisional survey khatian vide Appeal Case No 28876 of 1982. Out of the purchased lands of the plaintiff .30 acre as mentioned in the schedule has been acquired by the Government vide L. A Case No 128 of 1983-84 (Misc. Case No 2 of 1984-85) for Gas line which was in the possession of the plaintiffs and the compensation money for the said acquisition has been assessed at Tk. 188442/-and that the plaintiffs are entitled to get the said compensation money and accordingly they filed a petition to the Land Acquisition Officer for getting the compensation money. It appears that the original defendant Nos. 1 to 3 who also claimed to have purchased some land of the R. S Khatian from said Syed Ali and Gura Meah lodged a claim for the compensation money, besides some other groups of peoples have also applied for getting their alleged shares in the compensation money and the Land Acquisition Officer after hearing all the parties passed his order on 12.10.1985 and awarded compensation to only defendants 1 to 3 and hence the present suit by the plaintiffs. 

4. Now it appears that there are two grounds of contesting defendants in the suit namely defendants No 1 to 3 in one group and defendants No 6-12 in the another group and both the above groups have filed separate written statements, to contest the suit denying all the material allegations in the plaint, contending interalia that the suit is not maintainable, that there is no cause of action the suit is barred by limitation and also by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, waiver, estoppel and acquiescence; that the plaintiffs have got no right, title and interest or possession in the suit land and they have no right to the compensation money etc. that the suit is liable to be dismissed with cost. Besides both the groups of defendants claimed their own right, title and possession in the suit land and hence claimed their right to the compensation money of the L.A. Case. Apart from filing the written statement the defendant Nos. 6-12 instituted another suit being other suit No 171 of 1985 as plaintiffs on 23.11.1985 in the same court of the Subordinate Judge, Chittagong praying for a declaration that they are only entitled to get the compensation money assessed for the suit lands in L.A. Case No 128 of 1983-84 as described in the schedule below. The Court passed an order for hearing of both the suits together and date was accordingly fixed for evidence on 18.3.1995. The plaintiffs of suit No 169 of 1985 examined one Omar Faruque Chowdhury as P.W. 1 who proved some documents which were marked as Exhibits. Then' a question came up which of the two groups of the contesting defendants would cross examine the P.W. 1 first. The defendants 1-3 made a prayer by an application that defendant Nos. 6-12 should be asked to cross examine the said P.W.1 first as they as well as the plaintiffs of the suit are opposing the claims of the defendant petitioners. The learned Subordinate Judge then neared both the sides on the said point and thereafter asked the first group of the defendants namely defendant Nos. 1-3 to cross examine the said witness P.W.1 by his order dated 18. 3.1995. The defendants No 1-3 being aggrieved by that order filed an application under section 151 C.P.C. before the learned Subordinate Judge to reconsider the order dated 18.3.1995 and to ask the defendants 6-12 to cross examine the witness first alleging interalia that unless defendants no 6-12 are asked to cross examine first, the defendants Nos. 1-3 will be seriously prejudiced in their defence, particularly when the said defendant Nos. 6-12 have not denied the title of the plaintiffs of suit No 169 of 1985 in the other suit No 171 of 1985. The learned Subordinate Judge then heard both the sides of the said application but rejected the same by his order No 112 dated 2.4.1995. Now being aggrieved by the aforesaid two orders the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 along with the substituted heirs of defendant No 2 who died subsequently have filed this application before us. 

5. Mr. Saifuddin Ahmed Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners contends that the learned Subordinate Judge has committed error of law in asking defendant Nos. d-3 instead of defendants 6-12 to cross examine P.W.1 first and illegally passed the impugned order dated 18.3.1995 and also the order dated 2.4.1995 as a result the defendants petitioners have been seriously prejudiced and there has been failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that when there are 2 sets of defendants to contest the suit and if one set of defendants goes to support the claim of the plaintiffs wholly or in part, then in that case that set of defendants should be asked to cross examine the witness of the plaintiff first. His further submission is that in the instant case the contesting defendants 6-12 are in fact partially supporting the case of the plaintiffs; hence they should be asked to cross examine the. P.W.1 first. But the learned Subordinate Judge instead of asking them to cross examine P.W.1 has most illegally asked the defendant Nos. 1-3 to cross examine the said witness first and as a result there has been miscarriage of justice. In support of this contention Mr. Chowdhury has relied on 2 decisions, one reported in 32 ILR Bombay series at page 599 in the case of Haji Bibi Vs. H.H Sir Sultan Mahomed Khan and others wherein it has been held: 

"The word plaintiff means every person asking relief against another person.

"The plaintiff and such of the defendants as support the plaintiffs case wholly or in partly, must address the court and call their evidence in the first place, and then following the words of section 180 of the Civil Procedure Code the other party namely the persons opposed to the plaintiffs case and that of the other defendants supporting the plaintiff, must address the court and call their evidence. 
6. The other decision relied on by the learned Advocate for the petitioners is in the case of Shah Harilal Hamitalal and others Vs. M.G. Pathak and others reported in A.I.R.1964 Gujrat 26 wherein it has been held in para 3. 

On the question of right to begin and the question of leading evidence, we have provisions in order 18, rule] C .P .Code which reads as follows: 

The plaintiff has the right to begin unless the defendant admits the facts alleged by the plaintiff and contends that either in point of law or on some additional facts alleged by the plaintiff, the plaintiff is not entitled to any part of the relief which he seeks in which use the defendant has the right to begin. 

Sub-rule (2) of Rule 2 of order 18 C.P.C. reads thus: 

The other party shall then state his case and produce his evidence (if any) and may then address the court generally on the whole case. 

4) So far as the defendants go, the question which of the defendants should begin has not been dealt with in order 18 C.P.C. But on general principle, if any of the defendants supports the plaintiffs in whole or in part, then he should address the court and lead his evidence first before the other defendants who do not support wholly or in part the plaintiff's case. The order in which defendants lead evidence becomes important only when some of them support the case of the plaintiffs in whole or in part while the others do not if all the defendants completely oppose the plaintiffs case, then the question of order of leading evidence amongst the defendants is immaterial. It is only when the defendants are divided into two groups,, one group consisting of the defendants supporting the plaintiffs case in part and the other group consisting of the defendants who do not support the plaintiffs case in any part that the question of order of leading evidence becomes important. In such cases among defendants the order of leading evidence should be as follows: 

1) Those defendants who fully support the case of the plaintiff 
2) Those defendants who partly support the case of the plaintiff. 

3) Those defendants who do not support the case of the plaintiff in any part. 

7. Now, let us examine the instant case in the light of the above decisions cited before us. The learned Advocate for the petitioners has placed before us a certified copy of the plaint of other suit No 169 of1.985 and the ordinary copy of the 2 sets of written statements of defendant. Nos. 1-3 and defendant Nos. 6-12. On perusal of the written statements of the 2 sets of defendants, we find that both the sets of defendants have equally challenged the claim of the plaintiffs in the instant suit in which P.W.1 has been examined by the plaintiffs and at this stage it is difficult to say only from a reading of the written statements that the group of defendant Nos. 6-12 is at all supporting either wholly or in part the claim of the plaintiffs Now in our view so far the order in production and examination of witnesses in a case either civil or criminal it is the absolute discretion of the court concerned unless there is any specific law or rule therefor. In this regard we may look at section135 of the Evidence Act in chapter X . Section135 of the Evidence Act runs thus:- 

"135. The order in which witnesses are produces and examined shall be regulated by the law and practice for the time being relating to Civil and Criminal Procedure respectively and in the absence of any such law, by the discretion of the court. 

For the above we are of the view that a judge must necessarily be invested with a wide discretion in regard to ordering or permitting an alternation of the ordinary rules of practice and procedure at trials and the time and order in which the evidence shall be introduced. These rules are always subject to be modified in their application to particular case at the discretion of the Judge While counsel has discretion, the court has also power under this section to direct the order in which witnesses cited by a party shall be examined. 

Admittedly there is nothing in the code specifically as to which of the defendants should cross examine any prosecution witness first and hence in the above circumstances a court is to fall back on section 135 of the Evidence Act which speaks of the discretion of the court to fix the order of production and examination of witnesses, of course such discretion should be exercised judicially and not arbitrarily in the facts and circumstances of each case. In the instant case, as we have observed that from the reading of the written statements of the 2 sets of defendants it does not appear that the group of defendants 6-12 is supporting the plaintiffs claim either wholly or partially; hence the decisions relief on the learned Advocate for the petitioners cannot be of any help to his clients. Had it been a vase that the defendants 6-12 were supporting the plaintiffs claim wholly or partly in the written statement then possibly it could be said that unless defendant Nos. 6-12 were examined first then defendants 1-3 would have been prejudiced. But what we see at this stage on scrutiny of the written statements is that the case is a different one. From the impugned order we also find that the learned Subordinate Judge after hearing both the side decided in the facts and circumstances of The case to ask the defendants 1-3 cross examine the witness of the plaintiff first in Suit No 169/1985. As we have already pointed out that in the absence of any specific law, rules procedure, it is the discretion of the court concerned to order production of examination of a witness, we think that the learned Subordinate Judge has exercised his discretion judiciously and not arbitrarily. Further merely non making of the plaintiffs of the present suit as party defendants in other suit No 1.71of 1985 as alleged by the petitioners cannot be a ground for holding that the defendants 6-12 arc supporting the case Of the plaintiffs in T.S. No 169 of 1985. 

8. However for the reasons stated above, we find no substance in this revisional application and the same is summarily rejected. But before parting with this application we like to observe that if it transpires subsequently from the case and  conduct of the defendants No 6-12 that they are going to support the plaintiffs claim either wholly or partially, in that case certainly they should be steed to cross examine the witness of the plaintiffs first before the defendant petitioners. 

Let a copy of this judgment and order be transmitted to the court below at once. 

End.
